title: Collaborative Document Editor
summary: Design a browser-based document editor where many people edit the same rich-text document at once, see each other's cursors live, and always end up with identical content.
statement:
You are designing **a browser-based collaborative document editor**, similar in spirit to the word processors teams use to write specs, meeting notes and proposals together.

**Core journeys**
1. **Create and open** documents with rich text: headings, bold/italic, lists, tables, links and inline images.
2. **Co-edit** — several people edit the same document at the same time. Each person's typing appears on everyone else's screen within a fraction of a second, and everyone ends up with exactly the same document, even when two people type into the same sentence at the same moment.
3. **Presence** — collaborators see who else is in the document, with each person's cursor and selection shown in their colour.
4. **Sharing** — the owner shares a document with specific people, or with "anyone in the company with the link", as viewer or editor. Viewers see changes live but cannot edit.
5. **Offline** — someone on a flight keeps editing; when they reconnect hours later, their changes merge in without overwriting anyone else's work.
6. **Version history** — users browse earlier versions ("Tuesday 10:42 — edited by Asha"), see what changed, name a version and restore an earlier one.

**Clarifications from the interviewer**
- Typing must feel instant locally — the editor may never wait for a server round trip before showing a keystroke.
- Most documents have 1–3 people editing at once, but company-wide documents (all-hands notes, incident docs) can have 200 editors and thousands of viewers at the same time.
- Documents can grow to the length of a long book and accumulate years of edits.
- Once the editor shows "saved", a change must never be lost.

Cover requirements, estimates, API (including how editors exchange changes in real time), data model and architecture, then dive into conflict resolution and the scaling challenges.
scaleHints: 30M DAU; ~2M documents open at peak with ~3M concurrent editing sessions
~1M edit operations/s at peak across all documents (keystrokes batched every ~100 ms)
Typical document holds 50 KB of content; the maximum is ~10 MB
Hot documents: up to 200 concurrent editors and 5,000 concurrent viewers
Remote edits visible to other collaborators within 200 ms at p95 (same region)
Fine-grained version history kept 30 days; named versions kept forever
constraints: All copies of a document must converge to identical content regardless of the order in which edits arrive
No edit may be lost once it is shown as saved
Permissions are enforced on the server for every change; viewers can never inject edits
Offline sessions lasting several hours must merge without manual conflict resolution
outOfScope: Spreadsheets, slides and other document types

keyFunctionalRequirements: Create, open and edit rich-text documents
Real-time concurrent editing with automatic conflict resolution and convergence
Presence: live collaborator list, cursors and selections
Offline editing with merge on reconnect
Version history: browse, diff, name and restore versions
keyNonFunctionalRequirements: Instant local echo; remote propagation < 200 ms at p95
Guaranteed convergence and durability of acknowledged operations
~1M ops/s aggregate; hot documents with 200 editors and 5,000 viewers
Fast load even for long-lived, heavily edited documents
High availability; sessions recover transparently after a server failure
coreEntities: Document: doc_id, owner_id, title, created_at, latest_snapshot_ref, latest_seq
Operation: doc_id, seq (server-assigned), client_id, client_seq, base_seq, payload, author_id, ts
NamedVersion: doc_id, seq, name, created_by, created_at
Presence (ephemeral): doc_id, user_id, session_id, cursor/selection, colour
keyComponents: Collaboration servers holding WebSocket sessions, with routing so each document's sessions reach its owning server/partition
OT transformation engine or CRDT merge logic on client and server
Durable append-only operation log per document with server-assigned sequence numbers
Snapshot/compaction service writing periodic document snapshots to blob storage
Ephemeral presence channel (not persisted) with throttled cursor broadcasts
Version history service built from snapshots plus the op log
Viewer fan-out tier for read-only subscribers of hot documents
deepDiveTopics: OT vs CRDT: central sequencing vs peer merge, metadata/tombstone overhead, offline friendliness, rich-text complexity
One authoritative owner per document: routing, leases and failover, recovering in-flight operations
Op log plus snapshots: compaction policy and fast loading of heavily edited documents
Scaling hot documents: batching ops, throttling presence, separate fan-out for viewers
Offline merge and reconnection: idempotent resend of unacknowledged ops keyed by client_id + client_seq
commonPitfalls: Last-write-wins on whole documents or paragraphs, losing concurrent edits
Locking paragraphs or sections, which defeats real-time co-editing
Saving the entire document on every keystroke
Persisting cursor and presence updates in durable storage
Sending editors of the same document to arbitrary servers without coordination
Never compacting the op log, so opening old documents replays millions of ops
